reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: Renal artery stenosis is a narrowing of one or both renal arteries that can cause secondary hypertension and, when bilateral or affecting a single kidney, progressive ischaemic nephropathy
Atherosclerosis accounts for the great majority of cases, typically in older patients with widespread vascular disease, while fibromuscular dysplasia is the main cause in younger women
Clues suggesting a renovascular cause include hypertension of abrupt onset or that is severe or resistant, an abdominal bruit, and unexplained kidney asymmetry
A significant rise in creatinine after starting a renin-angiotensin inhibitor, especially with bilateral disease, is a classic pointer to renovascular disease
Recurrent flash pulmonary oedema without a clear cardiac cause can be a manifestation of severe bilateral stenosis
Non-invasive imaging such as duplex ultrasound, CT angiography, or MR angiography is used for diagnosis, with catheter angiography reserved for when intervention is planned
Medical therapy with renin-angiotensin blockade, other antihypertensives, statins, and antiplatelet treatment is the foundation of management for atherosclerotic disease

Revascularisation is reserved for selected patients such as those with fibromuscular dysplasia, rapidly declining function, refractory hypertension, or recurrent pulmonary oedema, since routine stenting has not shown benefit over medical therapy in most atherosclerotic cases
reference.pathophysiology: Renal artery stenosis reduces perfusion pressure to the affected kidney, which the kidney interprets as volume depletion and responds to by activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. The resulting angiotensin-mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone-driven sodium retention raise systemic blood pressure. When only one kidney is affected, the contralateral kidney can excrete the retained sodium, so hypertension is predominantly renin-driven. With bilateral disease or a single functioning kidney, sodium and volume retention dominate and drive the hypertension. Chronic hypoperfusion also causes ischaemic injury with tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and glomerulosclerosis, producing ischaemic nephropathy. Renin-angiotensin blockade can precipitate a fall in glomerular filtration because efferent arteriolar tone, needed to maintain filtration pressure in the underperfused kidney, is removed.
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound of the renal arteries with velocity measurements
CT or MR angiography to define the anatomy of the stenosis
Assessment of renal function and kidney size asymmetry
Monitoring of creatinine after introduction of renin-angiotensin blockade
Catheter angiography when revascularisation is being considered
Screening for other secondary causes of hypertension when appropriate
redFlags: Rapidly deteriorating renal function, particularly after starting renin-angiotensin blockade
Recurrent flash pulmonary oedema without a cardiac explanation
Severe or resistant hypertension unresponsive to multiple agents
Acute kidney injury suggesting critical bilateral stenosis or renal artery occlusion
reference.prognosis: Fibromuscular dysplasia generally responds well to angioplasty with a good chance of improving or curing hypertension. Atherosclerotic disease reflects generalised vascular disease and carries substantial cardiovascular risk; for most such patients optimal medical therapy gives outcomes comparable to intervention, and prognosis is driven largely by comorbid cardiovascular disease and the degree of established ischaemic nephropathy.
pitfalls: Reflexively stenting atherosclerotic lesions when evidence favours medical therapy for most patients
Stopping renin-angiotensin blockade for a modest, stable creatinine rise that is actually acceptable
Missing fibromuscular dysplasia as a curable cause of hypertension in a young woman
Failing to recognise bilateral disease as the cause of recurrent flash pulmonary oedema
management: Optimal medical therapy is the foundation for atherosclerotic disease, combining a renin-angiotensin inhibitor for blood pressure with a statin, antiplatelet agent and smoking cessation
Monitor serum creatinine closely after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, and reconsider revascularisation if function falls sharply, especially with bilateral disease or a single kidney
Add further antihypertensives to achieve target blood pressure where a single agent is insufficient
Offer percutaneous transluminal angioplasty, usually without stenting, for fibromuscular dysplasia, which frequently improves or cures the hypertension

Reserve angioplasty with stenting for selected atherosclerotic patients, notably those with recurrent flash pulmonary oedema, rapidly declining renal function or hypertension resistant to full medical therapy
Surveil renal function and kidney size to detect progressive ischaemic nephropathy
Refer to nephrology and vascular or interventional services for revascularisation decisions and screen for other secondary causes of hypertension where appropriate
